paper.title: Language to Rewards for Robotic Skill Synthesis
paper.central_claim: Using LLMs to define reward parameters that a real-time optimiser (MuJoCo MPC) turns into motion, via a Motion Descriptor and Reward Coder, enables interactive synthesis of diverse locomotion and manipulation skills; it reliably tackles 90% of 17 designed tasks versus 50% for a primitive-skill Code-as-Policies baseline.
paper.scope_decision: in_scope (A): frozen GPT-4 reward-translator harness whose reward code MuJoCo MPC optimises in closed loop for a simulated 12-DoF quadruped and a 27-DoF arm-hand; a real mobile manipulator is shown qualitatively.

preliminary_judgment: Written after reading the fixed text, before opening this paper's seat records: system_method; 17 author-designed tasks (9 quadruped, 8 dexterous) x 10 GPT-4 samples x 50 MJPC rollouts; the headline 90% vs 50% is a best-of-N (pass@10) task coverage that picks the best code with the same success evaluation, not a per-sample success rate; several quadruped criteria qualitative; per-task values figure-only; Reward-Coder-only ablation and an author-built CaP primitive baseline with the same GPT-4; templates/residuals co-designed per morphology with the evaluated tasks and simulator GT state; real robot two tasks by video without counts; cost unreported. Expected online (no transfer), scoped; holdout weak.

gap.author_gap: LLM robot interfaces rely on semantic planning or hand-engineered primitives, so expressiveness is bottlenecked by primitive breadth; low-level actions are hardware-specific and under-represented in LLM training data.
gap.checked_gap: Against a CaP baseline using authors-designed primitives, the reward interface solves more tasks in simulation (11/17 categories significantly higher, others comparable; 90% vs 50% best-of-N). The reward vocabulary and morphology templates are themselves hand-engineered, so the primitive bottleneck is relocated rather than removed.
lineage: Code as Policies / SayCan (LLM over primitives) and learned language-to-reward models -> Language to Rewards (LLM-defined reward parameters + real-time MPC)
LLM-as-reward-function in RL (per-rollout queries) and AutoRL (no language interface) = neighbours on the reward side

closest_adjacent.name: LLM-as-reward (Kwon et al., Hu & Sadigh)
closest_adjacent.unsolved_per_authors: large number of LLM queries per training

gap.residue: Dependence on per-morphology templates and a predefined residual set; ground-truth state in simulation; time-varying rewards unsupported.
gap.stakes: Data-free, interactive synthesis of dynamic locomotion and dexterous manipulation skills from language.
gap.method_response: Use rewards as the interface, split translation into template-filling and reward coding, and let MJPC compute actions online.
gap.remaining_gap: Template/term engineering, language-only specs, real-world evidence (authors); no per-sample reliability numbers in text, no counted real trials (ours).
gap.unresolved: Neighbour papers not pinned; whether the gain comes from MPC or the reward interface (versus CaP with a comparable optimiser) is untested.
gap.aggregate_note: son55 gap retained, including its own observation that the primitive bottleneck is relocated into a hand-designed reward vocabulary; this is why G is 3.

assessment.evidence_level_reason: Closed-loop simulation with state-based success on two embodiments. Not transfer: the real-robot part has no trial counts (EVIDENCE rule 1, E19), and the cross-embodiment reading is blocked by rule 2, because templates, reward terms and prompts were built per embodiment on the evaluated tasks (same reasoning as DEPS cross-domain instances).
assessment.author_claim_preserved: Using LLM-defined reward parameters optimised by MuJoCo MPC, the method reliably tackles 90% of 17 designed tasks while a primitive-skill Code-as-Policies baseline achieves 50%, enables interactive behaviour creation, and is validated on a real robot arm where non-prehensile pushing emerges.
assessment.strongest_supported_claim: In simulation on 17 author-designed tasks, a GPT-4 translator that writes parameters for a predefined set of reward terms optimised by MJPC covers more tasks than an author-built primitive CaP baseline when the best of 10 generated programs is taken, and the structured motion description helps reasoning-heavy tasks. Per-sample reliability, generality beyond the residual menu and real-robot success are not established.

independence from co-designed templates and reward terms

unresolved: per-task and per-sample numbers are figure-only (Fig 4/8/9; not scored)
LLM sampling settings for the 10 responses unstated

G.reason: Resolved toward sol (son55 4). Specific, sourced bottleneck: LLM robot interfaces are bounded by the breadth of hand-engineered primitives and LLMs cannot emit low-level commands. The lineage is clear (CaP, learned language-to-reward models, LLM-as-reward, AutoRL) and CaP is tested. Not 4: the method answers the "expert-engineered primitives" bottleneck with an expert-designed residual menu and per-morphology motion templates whose CHOICE lists enumerate the scene objects (agg:E004, son55:E028), so the residual gap is moved rather than bounded; the language-to-reward neighbours are not run.

M.reason: Resolved toward sol (son55 4). Reward-as-interface plus a structured motion descriptor gives reconstructible operations and distinguishable predictions that are probed: CaP stalls beyond its primitives, and Reward-Coder-only forgets approach terms. Not 4: the load-bearing assumptions are weak against the problem as posed. Expressivity is capped by a predefined, weight-tuned residual menu and per-morphology templates (the kind of expert design the gap criticises), and MJPC needs a full MuJoCo model with ground-truth object state in simulation (agg:E003).

X.reason: Resolved toward sol (son55 4). Full prompts, reward APIs, residual tables with weights, planner choice per embodiment, sim2real regulariser and the state-estimation pipeline are given. Not 4: the LLM sampling settings for the 10 responses and the MJPC configuration are not stated, yet the headline stability/pass-rate results depend on both; several task success predicates have no threshold (agg:E002); the real-robot implementation is a sketch.

measurement.reason: Resolved toward sol (son55 3). Each task-method gets 10 reward programs x 50 MJPC rollouts with simulator-state success. But the headline 90% vs 50% is a best-of-N task coverage, where the best of 10 programs is chosen with the same success evaluation (agg:E006); per-task rates exist only in figures; several quadruped predicates are undefined ("reach a fast turning speed", "remain flat", "keep balance"); and the real-robot claim has no counts. Anchor v2: undefined success criteria -> <=2.

causality.reason: Both seats 2; confirmed. Same GPT-4 and the same 10 samples for Reward-Coder-only and an author-built CaP baseline give relevant contrasts. Interface and controller are confounded (MPC vs unspecified primitive executor), CaP's primitives/prompts are the proposers', reward terms were designed with the tasks, one LLM only, no controller ablation, and "significantly higher on 11/17" has no stated test (agg:E005).

holdout.reason: Resolved toward son55 (sol 2). There is no held-out task, scene or embodiment. The 17 tasks, motion templates, reward vocabulary and prompts are co-designed per morphology; the best-of-N metric selects on the evaluated outcome; and the real-robot demonstration has no counts (E19), so it cannot carry retained-gain evidence. Two morphologies give breadth, but each has its own engineered harness (as with DEPS cross-domain instances). This lies between the anchor-0 (train/eval identical) and anchor-2 (development overlap with some separation) cases.

statistics.reason: Resolved toward sol (son55 3). The 10x50 design exposes translator and controller variance, but the dispersion is only in figures; the text gives no variance, CI or test (although it claims "significantly higher"), and failure attribution (translator vs controller) is qualitative.
